PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Pet Shop — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how to visit a pet shop like a kind person — and what every pet actually needs.

What is this?

A pet shop is a store full of animals and their supplies: fish in tanks, a dog in the window, a cat on a cushion, and shelves of food and toys.

What does it mean?

Pets are promises, not toys: every animal in the window needs food, a home and a kind family for its whole life.

What does the child need to know?

You need quiet voices (animals startle), gentle fingers (only where the shop says), and the honesty to know that looking is today’s job.

Why this matters

The pet shop is where families and animals meet — doing it kindly, and knowing what a pet needs BEFORE taking one home, is how good pets and good children happen.

What it teaches

Gentle-touch practice, empathy (what does the puppy need?), responsibility talk (feeding, walking, cleaning), and the difference between wanting and promising.

Words to learn

petpet shoppet storedogcatfishhamsterfoodadoptgentle

Say this to your child

“"The pet shop! Hello, dog in the window — hello, cat! Quiet voices... gentle fingers... Every animal here needs food, a bed and a kind family. Today we look. One day — a big promise!"”

Step by step

  1. Visit the window first — the dog and cat are the greeters, and they are working.
  2. Watch quietly: what is the puppy doing? What is the cat pretending not to do?
  3. Tour the tanks: fish, and the hamster on its wheel (a hamster runs up to five miles a night — on a wheel the size of a plate).
  4. Learn the shopping list: every animal needs food, a bed, water, and a vet — say it like a spell.
  5. Looking is free; adopting is a big promise. The pet shop teaches both, in one visit.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the paw-print sign hangs over the pet shop window where a dog and a cat look out at the street — the shop’s two official greeters, on duty every day.

Ask your child

"What does every pet need?" (food, water, a bed and a kind family) "What kind of voices do we use at the pet shop?" (quiet ones) "Is looking free?" (yes — adopting is the big promise)

What your child can say or do

Your child might name every animal in the window (twice, in case they forgot), run a stuffed-animal adoption agency with paperwork, or announce at dinner that the family’s future dog has already been chosen — by them, just now.

Out in the real world

American families say pet store; British families say pet shop — same window, same puppies. The visit is also the gentlest rehearsal for the real adoption talk: a pet is not a toy, it is a small promise kept every single day.

Try it together

Adoption day: every stuffed animal in the house lines up, the shop opens, and the customer picks one to "adopt" — with a promise to feed it, brush it and love it forever, signed with a crayon X.

Understanding check

Ask: "Is a pet a toy?" (no — a promise) "What do we use in the pet shop?" (quiet voices and gentle fingers)

This lesson pairs with the Pet Shop flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.
